title: Introduction to Computer Security
description: Learn GRE words through cryptography, secure software and networks, threats and defenses, incident response and forensics.

cards.definition: unruly; stubborn; unyielding; by extension, infeasible to solve efficiently
cards.sentence: RSA relies on factoring being intractable: multiplying two large primes is easy, but recovering them from the product is believed to be infeasible.
cards.explanation: No efficient classical factoring algorithm is known, and RSA keys of 2048 bits or more are considered safe against classical computers. Shor's algorithm could factor efficiently on a large quantum computer, which is why NIST has standardized post-quantum schemes such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204).

cards.sentence: If an attacker steals a private key, that single compromise can negate every protection the encryption was providing.
cards.explanation: Well-designed cryptography is meant to depend only on the secrecy of keys (Kerckhoffs's principle), so key generation, storage and rotation matter as much as the algorithm. Hardware security modules and operating-system keystores make keys hard to export.

cards.definition: capable of being shaped by pounding; impressionable
cards.sentence: Plain AES-CTR ciphertext is malleable: flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips the same bit in the plaintext, and nothing detects it.
cards.explanation: Encryption alone provides confidentiality, not integrity. Authenticated encryption modes such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 add a tag that makes tampering detectable.

cards.sentence: TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral Diffie–Hellman keys, so recorded traffic stays safe even if the server's long-term key is stolen later.
cards.explanation: Each session derives a fresh secret from temporary key pairs that are then discarded, a property called forward secrecy. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed static RSA key exchange for this reason.

cards.sentence: Deliberately slow, memory-hard password hashes such as Argon2 are a deterrent to offline guessing attacks.
cards.explanation: Fast hashes like SHA-256 let attackers test billions of guesses per second on GPUs. Argon2, scrypt and bcrypt use a per-password salt and a tunable cost, so every guess is expensive.

cards.sentence: Brute-forcing a 128-bit key is more than arduous: it would take about 3.4 × 10³⁸ trials in the worst case.
cards.explanation: Even at a trillion guesses per second that is on the order of 10¹⁹ years. Attackers therefore target weak passwords, poor random-number generation, or implementation bugs instead of the cipher itself.

cards.sentence: NIST sanctioned AES in 2001 as FIPS 197 after an open competition, which is why vetted standards are preferred to home-made ciphers.
cards.explanation: Kerckhoffs's principle says a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public. Algorithms that have survived years of open analysis are far safer than secret designs, so do not invent your own cryptography.

cards.sentence: TLS depends on the probity of certificate authorities, which is why a CA that misissues certificates can be removed from browsers' trust stores.
cards.explanation: A certificate binds a domain name to a public key and is signed by a CA. Browsers ship a list of trusted root CAs, and Certificate Transparency logs let domain owners spot misissued certificates.

cards.sentence: A digital signature lets a recipient confirm that a message is veracious: it came from the holder of the private key and was not altered.
cards.explanation: The sender signs a hash of the message with a private key (RSA-PSS, ECDSA or Ed25519) and anyone can verify it with the public key. Signatures provide integrity and authentication but do not hide the message.

cards.sentence: In DNS spoofing, an attacker races to deliver a mendacious reply that sends users to a server the attacker controls.
cards.explanation: Classic DNS answers are unauthenticated, so a forged answer that arrives first may be cached. DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS records, and randomizing query IDs and source ports makes forging harder.

cards.definition: something or someone misplaced in time
cards.sentence: Using MD5 or SHA-1 for signatures is an anachronism, since practical collision attacks exist for both.
cards.explanation: A collision is two different inputs with the same hash, which lets an attacker swap one document for another. SHA-1 was publicly broken in 2017 (the SHAttered attack); use SHA-256 or SHA-3 instead.

cards.sentence: A network that places tacit trust in every internal machine lets one compromised laptop reach everything else.
cards.explanation: Zero-trust designs drop the assumption that being inside the network means being safe. Each request is authenticated and authorized, and segmentation limits lateral movement.

cards.definition: penetrable; porous; allowing liquids or gas to pass through
cards.sentence: A firewall at the network edge leaves the perimeter permeable to attacks that arrive through phishing emails, stolen VPN credentials or a compromised partner.
cards.explanation: Firewalls filter traffic by rules on addresses, ports and sometimes application data, but they cannot stop an attack that uses an allowed path. Intrusion detection, endpoint protection and monitoring catch what filtering misses.

cards.sentence: Defense in depth means layers of controls that buttress one another, so the failure of one does not expose everything.
cards.explanation: For example, input validation, parameterized queries, least-privilege database accounts and network segmentation each limit the damage from the same bug.

cards.sentence: The principle of least privilege demands frugality with permissions: each user and program gets only the access its job requires.
cards.explanation: If an account is compromised, the damage is limited to what that account could do. Practices include separate administrator accounts, restricted service accounts and short-lived credentials.

cards.sentence: Social engineering is chicanery aimed at people rather than machines, such as a caller who poses as an employee to get a password reset.
cards.explanation: Attackers exploit trust and urgency. Defenses are largely procedural: verify identity through a separate channel, require approval for resets, and train staff to recognize pretexting.

cards.sentence: Phishing hunts for a dupe: a user who types a password into a fake login page hands it straight to the attacker.
cards.explanation: Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, such as FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, ties the login to the real site's origin, so credentials entered on a lookalike domain do not work. One-time codes, by contrast, can still be relayed by an attacker.

cards.sentence: In a SQL injection attack, crafted input insinuates extra commands into a query that the programmer meant to contain only data.
cards.explanation: Building a query by pasting user input into a string lets quote characters change the structure of the query. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) keep data separate from code.

cards.sentence: A Trojan horse dissembles as useful software, such as a free tool, while installing malware in the background.
cards.explanation: Unlike a worm, a Trojan does not spread by itself; it relies on the user to run it. Install software from trusted sources, verify signatures or checksums, and restrict who can install programs.

cards.definition: hide away or cache; produce and release a substance into an organism
cards.sentence: Developers sometimes secrete an API key in source code, thinking it is hidden, but anyone who can read the repository can read the key.
cards.explanation: Keys committed to Git stay in the history even after the file is edited, and automated scanners quickly find those in public repositories. Keep secrets in a secrets manager or environment variables, scan commits for them, and rotate any key that leaks.

cards.sentence: A perfidious insider with legitimate credentials can bypass perimeter defenses, so sensitive actions should be logged and sometimes need a second approver.
cards.explanation: Insider threats are hard to spot because the activity looks authorized. Separation of duties, audit logs and least privilege both limit and reveal abuse.

cards.sentence: After breaking in, attackers abscond with data by exfiltrating it, often slowly or over encrypted channels, to avoid triggering alarms.
cards.explanation: Data loss prevention tools, egress filtering, and monitoring for unusual outbound volume or unfamiliar destinations can reveal exfiltration.

cards.sentence: Banal passwords such as 123456 and password still top the lists of passwords found in breaches.
cards.explanation: Attackers try common passwords first, using leaked lists in password-spraying and credential-stuffing attacks. NIST guidance recommends screening new passwords against known-breached lists and allowing long passphrases instead of forcing arbitrary complexity rules.

cards.sentence: Users inured to constant security pop-ups click through them, including the ones that matter.
cards.explanation: Warning fatigue weakens any defense that depends on user decisions. Good design reduces false alarms, makes the safe choice the default, and saves interruptive warnings for real risks.

cards.sentence: Apathy about patching leaves known holes open: the 2017 Equifax breach exploited an Apache Struts flaw for which a fix had been available for months.
cards.explanation: Attackers scan the internet for unpatched systems soon after a vulnerability is disclosed. Keep an inventory of software, prioritize flaws known to be exploited, and test and deploy patches on a regular schedule.

cards.sentence: Evidence whose chain of custody is tenuous may be challenged or excluded.
cards.explanation: A chain of custody records who handled the evidence, when, and what they did. A hash such as SHA-256 recorded when a disk image is acquired can show later that the image has not changed.

citations.title: SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response (NIST)

cards.sentence: Forensic evidence can exculpate as well as incriminate: logs may show that a suspected employee's account was being used from another country.
cards.explanation: Investigators build a timeline from logs, file timestamps and network records, and look for evidence for and against each hypothesis instead of only what confirms the first theory.

cards.definition: characteristic of earlier times; primitive; unspoiled
cards.sentence: Forensic examiners work on a copy and use a write blocker so the original disk stays pristine.
cards.explanation: A write blocker prevents any writes to the evidence drive. Examiners take a bit-for-bit image, record its hash, and analyze the image. Volatile data such as RAM is captured first, because it is lost when power is cut.

cards.definition: mentally quick and observant; having insight
cards.sentence: A discerning analyst correlates events across firewall, DNS and endpoint logs instead of reading each in isolation.
cards.explanation: One log line often looks harmless, but a login from a new country followed by a new administrator account and a large outbound transfer tells a story. SIEM systems collect and correlate logs, and synchronized clocks (NTP) make timelines possible.

citations.title: SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management (NIST)

cards.definition: urgent situation; pressing needs or demands; state of requiring immediate attention
cards.sentence: An active ransomware outbreak creates an exigency, so the responder's first moves are to contain the spread and preserve evidence.
cards.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 (revision 2) describes the life cycle as preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Isolating affected hosts from the network limits spread, and powering them off can destroy evidence held in memory.

citations.title: SP 800-61 Rev. 2: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (NIST)

cards.sentence: Incident responders must apprise management, legal counsel and, when required, regulators and affected users.
cards.explanation: Many laws and contracts set notification deadlines. For example, the GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach, where feasible. A communications plan prepared in advance avoids improvising under pressure.

citations.title: Article 33: Notification of a personal data breach (GDPR)

cards.sentence: After a compromise, rescind the stolen credentials: reset passwords, revoke tokens and sessions, and revoke affected certificates.
cards.explanation: Changing a password does not always end an attacker's access, because session tokens, API keys and SSH keys can stay valid. Certificates are revoked through certificate revocation lists or OCSP.

cards.sentence: Responders need equanimity, because panicked actions such as wiping a server can destroy the evidence needed to learn what happened.
cards.explanation: Practiced playbooks and tabletop exercises prepare teams to follow a plan under stress. Keeping a timestamped log of every action lets the response be reviewed afterward.

cards.sentence: A blameless post-incident review helps ameliorate weaknesses by asking what failed in the process instead of who to blame.
cards.explanation: Lessons learned feed back into detection rules, patching, training and playbooks. Tracking root causes and fixes, with owners and deadlines, keeps the same incident from recurring.
